## Original problem

I share a flat with two friends. We keep arguing about ordinary household chores. Sometimes we agree on who will do something, but later we disagree about what the agreement meant. Our work schedules change, and one friend has started avoiding the conversations. What should I do?

BODY
I only have the problem statement here, plus the fact that a prior node was selected with an empty commitments surface. So I cannot lean on any earlier account of what the flatmates' agreement meant, and I should be explicit that anything I say about that is my own reading, not a recovery of a lost record.

The situation as stated has three interacting features. First, the friends sometimes reach agreement about who will do a chore, but later disagree about what that agreement meant. Second, schedules change, so whatever was agreed may no longer fit the circumstances in which it was made. Third, one friend has begun avoiding the conversations. These are not independent: avoidance makes renegotiation harder, and renegotiation is exactly what shifting schedules would seem to require.

A useful working hypothesis is that the recurring dispute is not mainly about willingness to do chores but about the scope and duration of an agreement. "I'll do the dishes" can mean this once, on my turn, or whenever they pile up; it can mean until schedules change, or until someone says otherwise. If the friends never fixed that, then later disagreement is predictable rather than a sign of bad faith. I do not know from the given material whether this hypothesis is correct; it is a frame for the next conversation, not a finding.

The avoidance matters separately. If one person is staying out of the conversations, pushing harder on the same format is likely to deepen the avoidance. It may help to make the conversation smaller and less accusatory: not "we need to settle the chores" but a short exchange about one recurring friction, at a time when nobody is rushing out. It may also help to put the outcome in writing in a form all three can see, because the disputed meaning is precisely what an unwritten agreement leaves open.

What I would not do is assume that the avoider is the problem. Avoidance often follows from conversations that feel like ambushes, or from being outvoted, or from having given up on being heard. The given material does not tell me which.

A concrete direction: propose a low-stakes review of two or three recurring chores, state each as a scope (what counts as done, over what period, and what happens when schedules change), and ask each person to correct the statement rather than defend a position. If that fails, the more honest question is whether the three of you can agree on a minimal baseline plus a renegotiation trigger, rather than on a fixed division.

I am uncertain about the diagnosis, the appropriate tone, and whether the third friend's avoidance is a symptom or a separate constraint. I also do not know the history of prior attempts, so I cannot claim that any of this is new or that it will work.
COMMITMENTS
Taking this up would involve treating the scope-and-duration hypothesis as a testable frame rather than a conclusion: the next conversation should try to elicit what each person understood a past agreement to cover, and whether the disagreement is about wording, about changed circumstances, or about something else. It would also involve accepting that the avoidance is a constraint on method, so any attempt to renegotiate has to be designed so that the avoider can participate without being cornered, and dropping the approach if it predictably increases withdrawal. A further commitment is to make the renegotiation trigger explicit, so that a change of schedule does not have to be litigated as a breach. What I am not committing to is the claim that the avoider is acting in bad faith, or that a written roster will resolve the conflict; both would need evidence this material does not provide. If the scope hypothesis turns out to be wrong, the fallback is to look for a different recurring structure in the disputes rather than to press the same frame harder.

{"body": "Put the two accounts side by side and the first thing that shows is that they are not answering the same question, and each is blind to something the other lights up. The body_route account works at the level of the procedure: what a written list does, whether a trigger point is really a trigger or only a precondition, whether asking about a concrete instance gives the three people anything shared. The commitment_route account works at the level of content: scope and duration, what 'I'll do the dishes' was understood to cover, whether the dispute is about wording or about changed circumstances or something else. Read together, they expose an assumption they share - that the disagreement is tractable by some change in format or framing - and a gap neither fills: neither says how you would tell, from inside the flat, which kind of dispute you are in.\n\nThat gap is where I would push. The body_route candidate wants a three-way distinction between specification ambiguity, performance disagreement, and schedule change, and admits the concrete-instance move does not make it diagnosable. The commitment_route candidate offers exactly the same three-way split - wording, changed circumstances, something else - and treats eliciting which one it is as the testable core. So both accounts converge on the same diagnostic need and neither supplies the discriminating test. That convergence is the more interesting object than either account's internal argument. It is also the place where the two accounts can be checked against each other: if scope-and-duration really is the recurring structure, then the concrete-instance question should surface it, because asking what a past agreement covered is asking a scope question. If it does not surface it, the commitment_route hypothesis is weakened, not just unconfirmed.\n\nOn the trigger point, I think the two accounts are closer than the body_route candidate allows. The commitment_route account makes the renegotiation trigger explicit as a goal - a change of schedule should not have to be litigated as a breach. That is the same worry the body_route candidate raises, seen from the content side rather than the access side. The body_route candidate's own worry that its point may simply restate the account's concession about willingness has a parallel here: if the commitment_route account already builds in a renegotiation trigger, then the access-set criticism is partly answered by design rather than by argument. I do not know whether that answers it fully; it shifts the question to whether a designed trigger is reachable by the avoider.\n\nOn avoidance, the accounts agree more than they seem to. The body_route candidate notes the danger that 'do you two think there is a problem?' is heard as an accusation. The commitment_route account names the same danger as ambush and treats the avoider as a constraint on method rather than as the problem. Both therefore commit to designing the conversation so the avoider can enter it. Neither provides phrasing that removes the risk, and I would not pretend otherwise.\n\nThe written list is the sharpest disagreement. The body_route candidate insists that demoting the list from load-bearing to incidental is a loss of a test rather than a neutral shift. The commitment_route account treats writing as a way to fix the disputed meaning, which is close to restoring the list to work. These cannot both be right in the same flat at the same time: either the writing is doing diagnostic work or it is only an artifact. The honest position is that this is an empirical question about this flat, not a settled point, and the two accounts disagree because they are guessing at the same unknown.\n\nWhat I would actually propose, if anything is taken up, is to use one conversation to run the commitment_route test - ask each person what they understood a past agreement to cover - and to watch whether the answers come apart along the wording axis, the changed-circumstances axis, or neither. That is a test of the scope hypothesis and a crude instrument for the three-way distinction at once. It is small, it is doable by one person, and its failure is informative: if nobody can articulate a scope, the frame is wrong and the body_route candidate's read that the problem is about access and avoidance gains relative weight.\n\nI cannot see the earlier contributions the body_route account reads, and I have only the problem statement plus the note of an empty prior commitments surface for the commitment_route side. So everything above is my reading of two characterizations, not a recovery of originals, and the convergence I am pointing at could be an artifact of both accounts being written from the same brief."}

Specifically, it commits me to the proposal that the scope-and-duration test and the concrete-instance question are not two moves but one, and that their shared failure mode - nobody can state what a past agreement covered - would count against the scope hypothesis and in favor of the access/avoidance reading. I do not have evidence that this single-test framing works in a three-person flat where one person is avoiding; it is a way to get information cheaply, not a validated method.\n\nIt also commits me to a specific reading of the disagreement over the written list: that the two accounts cannot both be right about whether the list is load-bearing, and that this is an empirical question about a particular flat rather than something to be settled by argument. I am not claiming the list is load-bearing; I am claiming the disagreement is real and unresolved.\n\nThe independent-intervention point carries over from the body_route side and I am not abandoning it: asking the other two whether they think there is a problem is itself an intervention, performed by one of the three, and nothing in either account removes the risk that it reads as an accusation. Any phrasing offered as a fix should be treated as untested.\n\nWhat I am not committing to: that the avoider is avoiding because of ambush, outvoting, or not being heard - the commitment_route account lists these as possibilities and the material does not choose among them; that a written roster resolves the conflict; that the trigger point is a genuine criticism rather than a restatement of an existing concession; that the concrete-instance move improves diagnostic yield at all rather than only changing the style of the answer.\n\nThere are dependencies I cannot discharge. My reading of the convergence presupposes that both accounts were written against the same problem statement and brief; if they were not, the convergence is manufactured. My claim that a single conversation could test the scope hypothesis presupposes that the avoider can be brought into that conversation without it being an ambush, which is exactly what is in doubt. The proposal that failure of the scope test strengthens the access reading presupposes that the two readings are alternatives rather than compatible descriptions of the same flat, and I do not know that they are.\n\nA later reader should not treat the scope test as validated, the list question as settled, or the convergence as established. The most I can say is that these are the points where the two accounts can be made to answer to each other, and that is where I would look next."}
COMMITMENTS
